title: Caramel custard tart
subtitle: a blind-baked sweet pastry case filled with a dark caramel custard baked until just set
excerpt: Caramel custard tart has a sweet pastry shell filled with a silky custard made from dark dry-heat caramel, cream, eggs, and egg yolks. The caramel gives the custard a deep, bitter-sweet flavour and a dark amber colour. The tart is baked in a water bath at a low temperature so the custard sets evenly without curdling.
sourceNotes: Baked caramel custard tarts draw on French patisserie traditions, related to the creme brulee and Portuguese pastel de nata. A deep, dry-caramel custard tart in this form became popular in British restaurant pastry in the 2000s, associated particularly with the work of chefs trained in French patisserie.

content.text: Caramel custard tart is a sweet pastry shell filled with a dark, rich custard made from caramelised sugar, cream, eggs, and yolks. The caramel must be taken to a very dark amber, which gives the custard its bitter depth. The filling is baked at a low temperature inside the pastry case, set inside a water bath to control the heat and prevent the custard from curdling.

Make, rest, and blind-bake the pastry in a 23 cm tart tin. Blind bake at 200 degrees C for 15 minutes with beans, then a further 5 to 8 minutes without, until the base is golden and dry. Allow to cool completely.

Make the caramel: heat the caster sugar in a medium heavy-based saucepan without stirring until it melts into a dark amber caramel. Swirl the pan as it colours. When deep amber (180 degrees C), carefully pour in the cream in a slow, steady stream; it will bubble up strongly. Stir until the caramel has dissolved into the cream. Add the salt.

Whisk the egg yolks and whole egg together in a large bowl. Pour the hot caramel cream over the eggs in a steady stream, whisking constantly. Strain through a fine-mesh sieve. Skim any foam from the surface.

Heat the oven to 150 degrees C (fan 130 degrees C / gas 2). Place the cooled tart tin in a deep roasting tin. Pour the custard into the tart case. Pour boiling water into the roasting tin to reach halfway up the sides of the tart tin.

Bake for 40 to 50 minutes until the custard is set at the edges and has a gentle, even wobble across the whole surface when the tin is moved. Remove from the water bath and cool at room temperature for 1 hour, then refrigerate for at least 2 hours before serving.

attrs.problem: Custard curdled and pitted rather than silky after baking
attrs.avoid: Avoid too high an oven temperature; the eggs scramble if they overheat.
attrs.fix: Use the water bath — it keeps the temperature around the tart below 100 degrees C. If curdling occurs, the oven was too hot or the tart was left in too long.

attrs.problem: Caramel seizing and solidifying when cream is added
attrs.avoid: Avoid cold cream; the temperature shock can cause the caramel to seize.
attrs.fix: Warm the cream gently before adding it to the caramel. Pour slowly and stir constantly. If it seizes, continue heating over low heat while stirring until the caramel dissolves back into the cream.
